The Home Depot · Curbside Pickup

The wait was short. The uncertainty was not.

In early 2020, contactless pickup had to work before every system caught up. I put arrival timing and check-in confirmation into the messages customers already received.

Role
Staff UX Designer
Scope
Field research, pickup email, and check-in messaging
Key decision
Make arrival timing a two-way signal between customer and store
Outcome
A 50-store, 60-day pilot reported clearer expectations and fewer calls to switch fulfillment

I — Inspiration

Customers could arrive without knowing what happened next

A customer could arrive, check in, and still wonder whether the store knew they were there. An average delivery time could describe operations without explaining that uncertainty. The problem was also about what happened between an arrival signal and a visible response.

Home Depot was building contactless pickup while operations and customer habits changed week to week. Associates, signage, and email carried much of the experience. Missing check-in feedback left customers unsure whether the store knew they were there.

I interviewed store managers, associates, and customers. Order complexity and store layout affected delivery time. Fulfillment changes disrupted the floor. Customers expected confirmation after check-in, but did not share one definition of “on time.”

Store-operations analysis and surveys gave us a starting point: customers expected delivery in under five minutes, average door-to-door time was 3.5 minutes, and 30% of pickup customers called to change their pickup method.

D — Design Process

The email became a way to share arrival timing

I framed the problem around missing feedback. Customers needed to know whether check-in worked and what to expect while waiting. Stores needed an arrival signal to help prioritize orders.

I designed those signals into the ready-for-pickup email and check-in confirmation. The flow needed explicit help and delay states, since successful check-in was not the only outcome.

E — Engagement

Connect the customer’s wait to the store’s work

Field interviews connected three perspectives: customers waiting for an order, associates preparing it, and managers coordinating the floor. A store’s layout and an order’s complexity affected the same promise customers were trying to interpret. The design needed to give both sides useful information without pretending every pickup was identical.

I used the missing-feedback problem to explain why expectation-setting belonged in the messages customers already received. An ETA could help the store prepare; a confirmation could tell the customer the signal had arrived. The point was a two-way exchange that supported the operation, rather than another instruction customers had to remember.

The constraint was a changing service with systems still catching up. I designed the pickup email and check-in messaging within that environment, keeping help and delay paths explicit. A successful check-in was only one state; an error or delay needed a useful response too.

A — Action

Check-in confirmation had to cover delays and errors too

The email explained when and where to collect, asked for an ETA, provided help and Spanish-language access, and avoided unrelated fulfillment options.

Check-in messaging covered success, errors that required a call to the store, and an associate-reported delay. Each state gave the customer an expectation or a recovery path.

A — Action

Confirmation was part of the service

The ready-for-pickup email was already a point of contact customers used. I brought timing and arrival choices into that message, alongside collection instructions, help, and Spanish-language access. Removing unrelated fulfillment choices kept attention on the pickup task.

The confirmation then had to answer the next question: what should I expect now? Success, a call-store error, and an associate-reported delay were different situations. Each needed an expectation or a recovery path. Designing those states together kept the experience from ending at the check-in button.

The reported pilot results should be read with the operational context intact. A 3.8-minute average with an ETA and a 4.5-minute average without one were both under the five-minute goal. They do not isolate the effect of my messaging from store preparation or other changes. The more useful result was the combination of reported expectations and fewer calls to switch fulfillment.

This was the same problem in two directions: the store needed an arrival signal, and the customer needed feedback. The message connected those needs without claiming to remove every source of delay.

S — Success

Clearer expectations in the store pilot

≈90%
Reported that pickup arrived when expected
3.8 min
Average door-to-door time with an ETA
<10%
Called to switch fulfillment, versus a prior baseline above 30%

Source: project presentation, 60-day pilot in 50 stores. Retrospective results have not been independently revalidated.

The presentation reports 4.5 minutes without ETAs. Both averages were under the five-minute goal; the figures do not isolate the effect of messaging from operational changes.

My takeaway: an arrival signal helps the store prepare, and a confirmation helps the customer wait. Both sides need feedback when the process changes.
